result: Full-length hIAPP preparations containing fibrils (aged 24 h) are significantly more cytotoxic to cultured pancreatic β-cells than preparations containing oligomers (aged 0 h), as measured by MTT reduction and caspase-3/7 activation. The cytotoxic species resides in the insoluble fibrillar fraction.
evaluation: Claims C20-C26 and C107-C109 provide converging evidence from multiple assays (ThT binding, TEM, dot blot, MTT reduction, caspase activation) demonstrating that fibril-containing preparations are cytotoxic while oligomer-containing preparations are not. The fractionation experiments (C26, C108, C109) strengthen the conclusion by localizing toxicity to the insoluble fibrillar fraction. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate tests.

result: The atomic structure of segment 19–29 S20G, determined by MicroED to 1.6 Å resolution, reveals pairs of parallel in-register β-sheets mated by a dry interface with tightly packed hydrophobic residues (Phe23, Ala25, Ile27), burying 265 Å² per strand with shape complementarity of 0.85.
evaluation: Claims C3, C29-C36, and C92-C95 collectively describe the structural determination and key features of the 19–29 S20G segment. The MicroED methodology is well-documented (C29, C71, C72, C82), and the structural parameters (buried surface area, shape complementarity, hydrophobic core composition) are quantitatively reported from the atomic model. Fiber diffraction validation (C33, C35, C36) supports the structure as representative of full-length hIAPP.

result: Segment 15–25 WT forms an arrangement of unmated anti-parallel out-of-register β-sheets that are structurally labile, completely disaggregating in 1% SDS with heat, while 19–29 S20G fibrils remain intact in up to 2% SDS.
evaluation: Claims C37, C101-C103 describe the atomic structure of 15–25 WT determined by MicroED (C30, C83), showing unmated sheets with small buried surface area (10.7 Å² per residue). The lability is experimentally demonstrated by SDS sensitivity assays (C38, C39) with both turbidity measurements and EM confirmation. The structural and stability differences between 15–25 WT and 19–29 S20G are well-supported.

result: Segment 19–29 S20G fibrils are cytotoxic to cultured cells, with toxicity comparable to full-length hIAPP at the same concentration (10 μM), inducing both metabolic dysfunction (MTT reduction) and apoptotic machinery activation (caspase-3). The S20G mutation confers significantly greater cytotoxicity than the WT segment.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 demonstrate cytotoxicity through multiple independent assays (MTT reduction, caspase-3/7 activation, FRET-based caspase-3 monitoring) with appropriate statistical analysis. The comparison between 19–29 S20G and 19–29 WT (C41) shows significant differences (p<0.0001), and the similarity to full-length hIAPP (C42, p=0.09) supports the segment as a model. Fractionation experiments (C43) localize toxicity to the fibrillar form.

result: Both spine segments seed full-length hIAPP fibril formation, but seeding with toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils produces more cytotoxic hIAPP fibrils with tighter packing (9.0 Å spacing) than seeding with non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils (10.0 Å spacing), causing hIAPP to adopt the structural and cytotoxic features of the seed.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C27, C49, C104, C105 demonstrate seeding capability and differential cytotoxicity outcomes with statistical support. The structural basis for differential toxicity is provided by fiber diffraction analysis (C51) showing different equatorial spacings. However, C106 is speculative about the mechanism. The seeds alone are non-toxic (C50), confirming the effect arises from seeded hIAPP structure. The conclusion that hIAPP adopts seed features is well-supported by converging structural and functional data.

result: Segment 19–29 S20G may serve as a model for the toxic amyloid spine of hIAPP based on shared structural features, cytotoxic properties, and response to inhibitors.
evaluation: This conclusion (C8, C53, C58) is supported by multiple lines of evidence: structural similarity via fiber diffraction (C33, C35, C36), comparable cytotoxicity (C42), similar mechanisms of toxicity (C55), enhanced toxicity with S20G mutation in both segment and full-length protein (C56), and similar response to EGCG (C57, C46, C47). The convergence of structural, functional, and pharmacological data provides strong support for this model.

result: Segments 15–25 WT and 15–25 S20G are not cytotoxic compared to full-length hIAPP fibrils, and do not induce caspase-3 activity.
evaluation: Claims C40 and C45 demonstrate lack of toxicity through MTT reduction and caspase-3 activation assays with adequate replication (n=12 across four biological replicates). The consistency across multiple assays and the contrast with toxic segments (C41, C44) support this conclusion. This finding is important for establishing structure-toxicity relationships.

result: Residues 15–29 were identified as the amyloid spine of hIAPP based on sequence differences between human and mouse IAPP, location of the S20G familial mutation, role of Phe15 in fibril formation, and ability of all four spine segments to form fibrils and seed full-length hIAPP.
evaluation: The identification of the amyloid spine (C73) is supported by multiple converging lines of evidence: sequence analysis (C74), mutation location (C75), prior functional studies (C76, C77), and experimental validation showing all segments form fibrils and seed hIAPP (C78, C27). This multi-faceted approach provides strong justification for the segment selection.

result: MicroED enabled structure determination of nano-sized 3D crystals (100-300 nm thick) of both segments, producing higher resolution diffraction (1.6 Å for 19–29 S20G, 1.4 Å for 15–25 WT) than microfocus X-ray crystallography on larger crystals.
evaluation: Claims C71, C72, C29, C30 demonstrate the technical advantage of MicroED for these peptide segments, with direct comparison showing superior resolution. The methodological details (C79-C83) are adequately described. This represents an important technical achievement enabling the structural studies, though it is a methodological rather than primary biological finding.

result: EGCG mitigates both 19–29 S20G and full-length hIAPP fibril formation and cytotoxicity, but does not affect 15–25 WT fibril formation, suggesting EGCG may target the hydrophobic dry interface.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 demonstrate differential effects of EGCG on toxic vs. non-toxic segments through EM and cytotoxicity assays with statistical support (C47: p=0.0004). The parallel effects on 19–29 S20G and full-length hIAPP (C57) support the segment as a model. However, the mechanistic hypothesis about EGCG binding to the dry interface (C120) is speculative, though reasonably supported by the differential effects on segments with and without hydrophobic cores.

result: Fiber diffraction analysis shows that 19–29 WT and S20G fibrils share similar structural features, and 15–25 WT and S20G fibrils share similar features, indicating the S20G mutation does not confer distinguishable fibril morphology from wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91 present fiber diffraction data showing similar reflections for WT and S20G variants within each segment pair. This is supported by radial profile analysis and consistent with prior literature (C115, C116). The conclusion that S20G does not alter gross fibril morphology (C91) is well-supported, though it contrasts with the significant differences in cytotoxicity and stability, suggesting the mutation affects more subtle structural features.

result: Both 19–29 S20G and 15–25 WT structures exhibit curved β-sheets, but with opposite functional consequences: in 19–29 S20G the curvature accommodates tight packing of the hydrophobic core, while in 15–25 WT it prevents sheet association.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 document the curvature in 19–29 S20G with quantitative RMSD analysis. The functional interpretations (C60, C61) are reasonable inferences from the structural data, though they remain interpretations rather than directly demonstrated mechanisms. The paradoxical opposite effects of curvature in the two structures represent an interesting structural observation, though the mechanistic explanations are somewhat speculative.

result: The S20G mutation adopts unusual backbone geometry (φ = −101.7°, ψ = 107.5°) creating a kink, and computational modeling suggests the 19–29 S20G structure has slightly lower energy than 19–29 WT (−590 vs. −535 REU).
evaluation: Claim C99 reports the observed backbone angles from the crystal structure. Claim C100 presents energy calculations from FoldIt modeling. While the structural observation is direct, the energy calculation depends on the accuracy of the computational model and the validity of modeling WT by adjusting the S20G structure. The energy difference is modest and should be interpreted cautiously, but the approach is reasonable for exploring potential structural differences.

result: Not all hIAPP fibril structures are cytotoxic; comparison with the out-of-register KDWSFY segment from β2-microglobulin suggests that solvation energy and presence of a dry interface, rather than simply in-register vs. out-of-register architecture, may determine cytotoxicity.
evaluation: Claim C59 is a reasonable inference from the differential toxicity of 15–25 WT (non-toxic) and 19–29 S20G (toxic). However, the comparison with KDWSFY (C62-C65) relies on a single literature example, and the proposed relationship between solvation energy and toxicity (C64-C65) is speculative. Claim C66 acknowledges uncertainty about the determinants of toxicity. More examples would be needed to establish the proposed structure-toxicity relationship definitively.

result: 19–29 WT fibrils are likely polymorphic and may contain some fraction structurally similar to non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils, which could explain their lower cytotoxicity compared to homogeneous 19–29 S20G fibrils.
evaluation: This is explicitly presented as speculation (C67, C69) based on prior literature showing polymorphism in related segments (C68). While the hypothesis is reasonable and could explain the intermediate toxicity of 19–29 WT, it lacks direct experimental support in the current study. The authors appropriately present this as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion, but it remains unvalidated.

result: Background claims establishing the association of hIAPP with Type-II Diabetes, the correlation between amyloid and β-cell loss, the non-amyloidogenic nature of mouse IAPP, and the pathogenic S20G mutation.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C9-C19, C52) provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. They set the context for the study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with the field's understanding.

result: The 19–29 S20G crystal structure contains a wet interface that does not represent the amyloid spine, as evidenced by smaller buried surface area (153 Å²), lower shape complementarity (0.64), presence of water molecules, and mismatch with full-length hIAPP fiber diffraction.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 describe the wet interface and provide multiple lines of evidence for why it does not represent the physiologically relevant amyloid spine. The fiber diffraction comparison (C86) is particularly compelling. This represents important negative data that validates the focus on the dry interface as the amyloid spine model.

result: Morphological characterization of spine segment fibrils and crystals by electron microscopy, showing that segments form various fibrillar structures including striated ribbons and 3D crystals, and that seeds do not bind ThT.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 provide morphological characterization of the various spine segments by EM. These are straightforward observational data supporting the formation of ordered structures. The observation that seeds don't bind ThT (C114) is important for interpreting seeding experiments. This represents standard characterization data.

result: The S20G mutation confers greater cytotoxicity within both segment 19–29 and full-length hIAPP.
evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by the cytotoxicity data comparing 19–29 WT and S20G (C41) and by literature citations regarding full-length hIAPP. This parallel effect in both segment and full-length protein strengthens the segment as a model and highlights the importance of the familial mutation.

result: Raising antibodies against hIAPP fibrils may represent a promising therapeutic strategy, based on recent success with anti-amyloid-β antibodies.
evaluation: Claim C70 is explicitly speculative ('may represent') and conditional ('if hIAPP fibrils truly are a major type of toxic aggregate'). While the analogy to amyloid-β is reasonable and supported by citation (Sevigny et al., 2016), this represents a future direction rather than a finding of the current study. The speculation is reasonable but unvalidated.
